content: The global strategic plan aims to strengthen existing initiatives by encouraging countries to take ownership of their rabies elimination efforts. This includes utilizing national elimination plans to achieve country-specific goals and ultimately reach the target of zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030. Objective 1: The plan focuses on the effective use of vaccines, medicines, tools, and technologies to reduce the risk of human rabies. This will be achieved through expanded dog vaccination programs, improved public awareness and education, and increased access to healthcare, medicines, and vaccines for at-risk populations. Objective 2: The plan emphasizes generating, innovating, and measuring impact through: 1. Developing effective policies, guidance, and governance by harmonizing international recommendations, frameworks, and strategies, while building capacity in countries. 2. Ensuring the availability of reliable data to support effective decision-making by promoting the use of technology and health innovations, refining tools for monitoring and reporting, strengthening surveillance systems, and integrating reporting mechanisms. Objective 3: Sustaining commitment and resources is critical. This will be achieved through multi-stakeholder engagement and by demonstrating the impact of activities conducted under the United Against Rabies collaboration in national, regional, and global rabies elimination programs. These objectives aim to ensure that dog vaccination programs are effective and comprehensive, that vaccines and information reach high-risk populations, and that dog bite prevention strategies are widely implemented. A secondary goal is to ensure the availability of trained professionals in human and animal health and education, alongside accurate and comprehensive rabies surveillance and program monitoring. The theory of change outlines the steps required to achieve zero human rabies deaths worldwide. It is built on three pillars: 1. Operational capacity-building to strengthen health systems. 2. Education and advocacy to prevent human rabies deaths. 3. Monitoring and evaluation to support global efforts. The logic framework translates the theory of change into actionable steps, describing key outcomes, outputs, and major activities required to achieve the Zero by 30 goal. The United Against Rabies collaboration, formed by the World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), and Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC), drives elimination efforts through the effective use of vaccines, medicines, tools, and technologies; reliable data for decision-making; sustained commitment; and effective policies, guidance, and governance. Rabies is 100% preventable, yet it kills over 59,000 people annually in more than 150 countries. The disease is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear. The global strategic plan prioritizes objectives defined in the theory of change to address this preventable tragedy. Key Strategies: 1. Education and Awareness: Increasing awareness and improving education about rabies are essential to encourage dog vaccination and prompt care-seeking behavior after exposure. Community engagement and global campaigns like World Rabies Day and End Rabies Now play a vital role in raising awareness. Future efforts will focus on locally relevant education campaigns, bite prevention strategies, and responsible dog ownership to sustainably prevent rabies in animals and humans. 2. Dog Vaccination: Vaccinating dogs is the most cost-effective and sustainable way to prevent rabies transmission between dogs and from dogs to humans. The plan includes developing best-practice guidance for implementing dog vaccination programs, conducting regional capacity-building workshops, and supporting countries with effective vaccination campaigns. This includes ensuring the availability of affordable, safe, and effective vaccines through biological banks, strengthening veterinary services, and promoting innovative approaches to reach free-roaming dogs. 3. Access to Healthcare and Vaccines: Timely and appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is nearly 100% effective in preventing rabies deaths. However, access to this basic care is limited in many endemic areas. Expanding access to high-quality, affordable PEP for at-risk populations requires robust health systems capable of reaching underserved communities. The plan supports national strategies to treat dog bites and rabies exposures, contributing to universal health coverage. It also advocates for the inclusion of rabies PEP in global vaccine investment strategies to ensure free access in low-income countries. 4. Effective Policies and Governance: Coherent international standards and guidance reflecting best practices in rabies control are essential. Countries need support to adapt these guidelines to their local contexts and to monitor, assess, and refine strategies for maximum impact. Training human and animal health professionals will strengthen the effective use of vaccines, medicines, and tools. Harmonized international recommendations will streamline a One Health approach into policy development, ensuring a consistent global strategy for rabies surveillance, diagnosis, and prevention. By implementing these strategies, the global plan aims to reduce human rabies risk, improve access to healthcare and vaccines, and validate rabies elimination in individual countries and regions. The ultimate goal is to achieve zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030.
